extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in number theory; interested general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and state the Baker–Heegner–Stark theorem giving the complete list of imaginary quadratic fields whose rings of integers are principal ideal domains (equivalently, have class number one), plus historical context and variants of the statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalence: class number one ↔ ring of integers is PID
rubrics_metrics.description: The class number of Q(√d) is one if and only if the ring of integers of Q(√d) is a principal ideal domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equivalence identifies the algebraic property (class number) with the ring-theoretic property (PID) for quadratic extensions Q(√d). It is the basis for phrasing the classification problem: determine those d for which the class number equals one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Baker–Heegner–Stark theorem (imaginary quadratic class-number-one list)
rubrics_metrics.description: If d < 0, then the class number of Q(√d) is one if and only if d ∈ {−1, −2, −3, −7, −11, −19, −43, −67, −163}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These specific square-free negative integers are the complete list of d for which Q(√d) has class number one; they are often referred to as the Heegner numbers. The theorem resolves the special case of Gauss's class number problem for imaginary quadratic fields.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminant form of the class-number-one list
rubrics_metrics.description: Equivalently, in terms of the field discriminant D of Q(√d), the fields with class number one correspond to D ∈ {−3, −4, −7, −8, −11, −19, −43, −67, −163}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some expositions prefer to state the list in terms of discriminants D rather than the square-free d; both lists describe the same set of imaginary quadratic fields up to the usual identification between d and D.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heegner numbers (terminology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The integers d in the above list (−1, −2, −3, −7, −11, −19, −43, −67, −163) are known as the Heegner numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The name 'Heegner numbers' is commonly used in the literature; some sources refer to the result as Heegner's theorem (or Baker–Heegner–Stark theorem) depending on historical attribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical attributions and proof methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Heegner gave an essential proof in 1952, which was not immediately accepted; Harold Stark published a proof in 1967 clarifying and completing aspects of Heegner's argument. Alan Baker provided an independent proof in 1966 using linear forms in logarithms and reducing the problem to finite computation. Later proofs and variants used modular functions and work of Gross–Zagier and Goldfeld also provided alternative approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article emphasizes that multiple proofs and approaches exist (Heegner's modular-function-based work, Baker's transcendence methods, Stark's exposition, and later modular-function or Gross–Zagier style proofs). Historical details include references to gaps, reconstructions, and subsequent variants (Deuring, Siegel, Chowla, Kenku, Chen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relation to Gauss's class number problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The theorem solves the special case of Gauss's class number problem for imaginary quadratic fields, i.e., determining which imaginary quadratic fields have a given fixed class number (here, class number one).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This situates the result within a larger program of understanding class numbers of quadratic fields; the article notes the theorem as the complete resolution for the imaginary quadratic class-number-one case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open case: real quadratic fields (d > 0)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is unknown whether there are infinitely many d > 0 for which Q(√d) has class number one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article contrasts the complete classification in the imaginary case with the unresolved real quadratic case, noting computational evidence that many such real fields exist but no proof of infinitude.
